blocks.x: Let's see. Today is November the 11th, isn't it? What is it? Yes, I want to see. Yeah, November the 11th, 1962. And I'm here. I don't even know where I am. You better tell me where I'm at. Bay St. Louis, Mississippi. And what's the street we're on, the address? 309 Esther Brook Street. Esther Brook Street in Bay St. Louis, yes. And could I get both of you's names? Sure. I'm Carmen, and he is Sumner Labatt. Sumner Labatt. And Carmen Labatt. And you're a man and wife? That's right. I've been for 41 years. 41 years. That's right. Mm-hmm. I see. Do you play, by the way? No, I don't. Oh, I better put my name on there, too. I'm Dick Allen. There's my name. That's so the people that hear this will know. Sure. Well, let me see, Mr. Labatt. When were you born? If you don't mind, tell us exactly. January the 23rd. January the 23rd. January the 23rd. 1894. And how do you spell your name? Last name? Mm-hmm. L-A-B-A-T. Just like The Undertaker in New Orleans. That's a cousin of mine. Oh, yeah. You know Danny Barker? Yeah. He was a youngster. He was born in 1990. He played guitar and banjo. No. His grandfather used to work for Labatt over there, and he'd tell about how they'd even have the horses crying on some of the funeral. That's right. What was that guy's name? Joe Never Smile or something? I had a fellow driving the horses, and he looked sad, and his horses would look sad, too. Uh, let me see now. How do you spell Sumner? S-U-M-N-E-R. Sumner Labatt. Let me see. Well, uh, let me start off now. We got where you were born, and we got when you were born, but not where. Right here. Next door to me. What's the address there? 307. And we're in 309 now. That's right. 309 Estabro. Uh, did your family play music? My daddy played baritone. What kind of baritone was that? I mean, how did it look? Did it start a baritone saxophone? No. The brass band. That's the brass band. Uh-huh. I see. What was the name of the brass band, by the way? Pro Moat. Pro Moat? Uh-huh. That's an organization, yeah, you see, society. Uh-huh. And they had their own brass band? Yeah. A good one, too. How many pieces?

I guess about, let me see, they had two trumpets, three trumpets, one baritone, one bass, snag drum, bass drum, and two trombones. How many pieces? How many pieces you didn't come to? I didn't come to that. That's about eight. Did you say tuba or no?
Yeah, tuba. What kind of, they had a clarinet?
They had no clarinet.

No, not then. They had a clarinet, I don't know. Saxophone. Old man Teo never did play in that band. Not playing, no. Uh-huh. Who's old man Teo? That's the name of the band. That's the Teo used to play with Peter Bukowski and his daddy.
His dad. He used to live here, you see. Born and raised here, Teo did.
There's papa and Lorenzo. Lorenzo's daddy. I think he was Lorenzo Junior. Yeah, I think so, but then they had another brother, papa. Yeah, another brother.
Louis. Louis.
Yeah.
He played too. Did you know both of them? Yeah, but I didn't know his brother played. My mother had to play after he left Big Xanny, because they left when they were young, you know.
And they were born and raised here. Right, yeah.
I see.
I heard they came from Mexico, but I guess they didn't.
I know when I was a young man, they used to be right there on Main Street, you know. Uh-huh. And I thought Teo had the Norella that was born and raised here myself.

Probably was. Yeah, I don't know. That's a Spanish name, you know. Maybe his people came from Mexico. Uh-huh. They might have, that's right. Or he might have gone back there to study for a year or something. Sure. And you never know. He did. He was a great musician. Come here. Here we go. Here's Harold. He didn't have it by him. Hello, can I have him? He's just telling us. Uh, this is Harold, Adrian. Remember who that? How do you feel? How you feeling? I'm fine, I'm fine too. It's fine, my boss. Uh, I wanna, uh, actually, you, wait a minute. What happened there? Well, we can check it. Yeah. Now, let's see. We're talking about Teo. Yeah, well, Papatio was over here, that's when Lorenzo was young. Yeah, that's right. You ran around your age, huh? Yeah. Uh-huh. I mean, you took lessons with Papatio while you were there?

You just started playing yourself? No, I, I taken a few lessons in school out in Virginia, you see. Wow. And when I came, I used to play a violin. But, uh, after the clarinet, I played a guy in our band. I resumed the clarinet, you see. Uh-huh. And I put the violin down. Oh, yeah. What was this, Virginia? I went to school out in Virginia. Where is this? Rock Castle, Virginia. About 40 miles from Richmond.
Taylor in school.
Taylor? Yeah, Taylor, by trade.
Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Let's see. Well, did, did you and Tio ever play together while he was in? No, I never did there with Tio. Oh.

But what, what sort of band you played with a long time ago? The Supreme Band was the band I played with. Uh-huh. And practically most of the fellas died and I formed my own band. That's why I started getting, uh, uh, fellas out of New Orleans to play with me. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. I'd get cornet and saxophone and play one or two musicians I'd get most of the time. Uh-huh. And I used to get Kid Rainey, Kid Howard, Kid Ricardo Alexis. Uh-huh. And, uh, I even had Celestan come out and try and play with me. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. And, uh, what's this year, a fella, he's playing with Moe Raymond's son-in-law. Moe Raymond? No. Whose son-in-law? Humphren. No, I hired Humphren to come out there and play with me too. Willie Humphren. Not sax, trombone.
No, I went up and played sax and clarinet both.

George, George, uh, uh, What did he play? He played trumpet. You know George, uh, George, uh, George McCollum? McCollum. That was my man trumpet player. George McCollum. Yeah, George McCollum, he used to come out there every weekend. We'd go down to Bilox and Gulfport on a boat excursion, you know, and play for excursions down there. What, excuse me, what kind of band did you have?

I had a six-piece band. Reading, faking, both or what? Both. Reading and faking. Some of them were fake, you know. You have a lot of arrangements? No. Not too many arrangements? Uh-uh, not too many. What were some of the tunes that you'd have arrangements of?
Well, we didn't have no special arrangement, tell you, it was mostly jazz.

Oh, mostly, mostly. Yeah. They could read, but you mostly played jazz. I see. Yeah, I see, because they used to think like George McCollum, he was an Indian-Oman musician. Yeah, he was a sight reader.

Yeah. And this fellow Johnny Hande, I played with him for years and years too, Johnny Hande, the saxophone player. He told me about you. He's Johnny Hande? He's playing, yeah. He's playing with me two or three nights a week, Johnny Hande.
But for the first time I ever played here, I played with you, I don't know.

It's been a long time ago. Oh, yeah, I was really young, son. Yeah, I played with pretty heavy musicians out in the, out in the, out in the, out in the old time musicians, you know. But I played with some mighty good ones.
Sure. The Supreme Band that was here? Yeah. That's right. Who was the members of it? Do you remember? Yes.

Every one of them did except me. Really? We had about seven of us. Who was the members of it? There was Armand Tweedo. What did he play? He played trombone. There was Babe Bennett. He played cornet. Paul Maurice played clarinet. I played the violin at that time. I was leading the orchestra, you see. And they had Manuel Alexander, he was the drummer. That's it? And Dota frozen boy, he played guitar. And Edward Anderson, he played the bass violin. That was the lineup we had. Yeah. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. He played the bass violin, that was the lineup we had.
Did Paul Maurice play any other instruments?
No clarinet, that's all.

Well who was the drummer named Maurice? Manuel Alexander, I mentioned his name. No, but there's a drummer named Maurice. From here. From here, huh? What? I'm not confused. I must be confused. You're confused. Yeah, I'm thinking he's a saxophone player or something. There's seven pieces we had. Oh yeah. Something, I must have them all mixed up, you know. I hear so many names in a day it's hard to keep them all straight. Yes sir.

Well there's a drummer in the island by the name of Norbert Maurice. This fellow, Paul Maurice, would play clarinet with our orchestra. He's his boy, Norman's uncle, you see. He used to play drum, he too, but he lives in the islands now.
What about the Supreme Band? When was it going?

Oh, that was going before World War I. I came here right after World War I and I joined them. I came here, you see. I just came from school and they didn't have no violin player. At that time they had the old Imperial Band in New Orleans. Mania Parade, I think. Yeah, Mania Parade. Well, not Peter. What's this your fellow?
P-Rong?
No, he played violin with him. Robichaud? Mm-mm. Who played violin with Manuel Parade?
Yeah.
Not Peter, not the one we were talking about.
I know Peter Bocas.
I know who it is and I can't say anything.
I'm trying to think of his name.
He used to play with Manuel in there.
I'll tell you. He co-played with him at that time. It's not Bocas.

It's something like that name, too. Well, to make a long story short, I was near a week from school. This fellow Paul Maurice, he was the leader of the band, leading with Clarinet, you see. And they came around, I read music, pretty good at the time, just out of school. And they brought some music in front of me to play on my violin just by myself. I said, well, I'm no sight of reading. I could sound better if I had some kind of compliment behind it, you see. So I played. I said, will you go anything like that? He said, that's fine. We want you to play in our band. Then he gave me a waltz to play. I said, I got him some of you. So I played the waltz. And I joined the band. I played with them until everyone died, practically.

How old are we to get your name down here? Some people don't know who you are. What is it? Well, Harold, there's on New Orleans, 5000 Mexico Street. Good. Yeah, we want to know. Now you say you were born here. That's right. And then you went up to Virginia about what year? 1950 then. Around 1950.

That's the time I got out, rather, I believe. Well, that's the time you got back. Yeah. Oh, you were out there for three years, four years, huh? Three, four years. So you were up there around 1980? No, you were out there from here. I even cried on the train.
Didn't know where I was going. Never lived in my life before. Didn't know where I was going.

What was it like up there in Virginia as far as music was concerned? Well, it was good. They had a brass band and they had an orchestra. And they had an orchestra, and I used to play second violin in the orchestra. And they had a professor from Richmond, Virginia to come up there and teach us twice a week, sometimes once a week. Well there were two of us who were playing violin in the orchestra at the time and the professor taking a light to me. And he said, boy I got music in you. And he started giving special lessons for his class violin player. So he gave me about a dozen lessons, private you see. And he said I'm the one who should be playing first violin instead of the leading violin player. And he'd be playing second because I could execute better than he could you see. But he could read music almost on sight you see. So I just continued playing second violin. When he left school that's where I started playing first violin you see.

There were some good musicians around in Virginia. I know that a lot of them, one fellow made a name for himself, went to New York, named Ward Pinkett but he died. I think he went to Hampton Institute. Yeah. I doubt if you'd known him, he's probably younger than you. We had an Italian professor up there, he was good. Professor Gadibasio was his name.

Gadibasio. Gadibasio was his name. And he was fun. We had a crack brass band up there. Oh yeah? Crack brass band up there. Readin'? Fakin'? Sure, I don't know fakin'. All readin'? You had to read all readin'. There was no fakin' in that. What about the brass band here?

What's the name of it? Promo Brass Band. Promo. All of those were readers too. That was all readin', your father and everybody. Every one of them were readers, good readers too. Who was in that band? We didn't get that either I don't think.
Yes sir. We had the Supreme Band.
Yeah but what were the names of the men?
Do you remember the men in the promo? Most of them I do.
One of them really in them too. Yeah I'd love to have them. That was my dad.

I don't know. I don't know. There was Joe Graves, Cornette Flair, B. Bennett, Cornette Flair, John Collins, Cornette Flair, Oscar Collins, Trombone, Almond Credo, Trombone. Mr. John Batiste, bass. And Emilio Pito, bass drum. I think Budda Slickham was a snare drum. I don't think they had no clarinet player in that band at that time.
Do they have any kind of peck horn, mellophone, alto, anything like that?
Yeah, they had alto. I'm trying to think if he was playing alto. Well Joe Graves, he was playing second corner, then he was taking up alto after he had three or four corners playing, you see. I see.

Well now, by what years would that be that these men played with the band? It's about, you know, this is around the time, you know. What's that? I guess. Was that before or how you went to that? That was before I went to a young boy then, you know. 1915. 14, 15. 14, 15. That was about 1912. 1912.

Yeah, they had a crack brass band and they used to practice in my daddy's dining room practice every Sunday. You couldn't get to yours, let know when the other people would be around listening to them. Not only listening, we'd come and dance. Dance to the brass band.
Oh yeah, they'd practice. They used to go to the Mobile and play for dances, the brass band. Would they buck the Excelsior over there?

Well, I don't know about bucking, but they used to play over there. Yeah. And the Excelsior had a good brass band then. I know, I heard about that. Yeah, they had a good brass band them times. My dad, he's one of the best baritone players they had on the coast. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. And a lot of times you'd go to New Orleans and play with some of them New Orleans bands. He's a good baritone player.
In them days you had to be good because most every brass band you played with in them
days they put that music on. That music in front of you. That's right. And every time they practiced it they had that music right in front of you.

Even rehocers. Sometimes some of them rehocers twice a week. Probably the Holy Ghost. Every Sunday. Every Sunday. On Tuesday and Friday. The Holy Ghost brass band. Yeah. Was that a school brass band? No. We used to practice up at the Holy Ghost Hall on Tuesday and Friday. And they named the band the Holy Ghost brass band. They used to play for the parade. And at that time you see Catholic had bands for the burial and everything. You know right? Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.

Any music left from the times of your father? No sir. I wish somebody had saved that. You remember any of the tunes, any of the numbers they played? No sir. What about you? What was the first tune you ever played? Sometimes those things come back to you. Yeah. Well, anything you played when you were starting, you ought to remember one or two numbers. Well, you ought to used to play a la da. Well, your theme song was three o'clock in the morning.
That's right. We'd be signing off. We'd play that, bye-bye Blackwood. We'd be playing because we started playing blackwood.
You ought to remember what one of the numbers you used to play? You know, one of the first numbers that you played? You know, you fired it. Oh yeah. You know what I played?
One of them? My favorite number was the St. Louis Blues. Oh yeah. Oh yeah?

That high society. Yeah. Oh yeah. That sounds like good bands they had over here. Yeah, yeah. Good band. Here, I'll close this. Oh. How you do? All right. Let's see. You all in any step? No, we just started. We went in. We're about in the middle of the way. We went in. You all in here, man? I'm fine. You all won't you just? You all won't you just? You all won't you? I came back. Hey, Governor. How's you, Jack? We got fun. I'm good, man. We got good memories, man. We're down as I am. Harry, say your name. You got good memories, man. We're down as I am. You got them. You got them. Okay? Say your name now now that you're here again. Say your name, Bonnie. Watch out. There you go. There you go. How about you? Joe Jackson. All right. Just so them know who came in. Joe Jackson. Patrick Stant. I have a bachelor. Wait. I looked you them all. Fine you. Good. We were just talking about the old numbers that you played. Excuse them the power. Sure the power. But the Supreme Band played some of those numbers that you're talking about. Yeah. And oh man, we've been through over so many things since they just got here. We talked about some of the musicians used to come over from New Orleans. What about the Supreme Band? Would they go to New Orleans as a unit, the whole band? They mostly on the coast. Mostly on the coast.

Where did you play? We played Mobile all along the coast, played at the old Great Southern Hotel. Practically every week before we went down in Gulf Coast, sometimes twice a week. Then we played Mobile a gang of times, Eureka Gordon and several other places. I forgot the names of them. You know Bunk used to play at the Great Southern Hotel.

Yes. He used to come over here. How long ago that Great Southern Hotel was born here? I heard him, but I don't know him. He's a trumpet player. He used to come over here. How long ago that Great Southern Hotel was born here? I didn't have to go to a long time ago. Long time ago. Let me see now. What years were you with the Supreme? Is that the band you joined right after you came by? Right from school, that's right. And how long did that band stay up with you in it? For years and years. I don't know. I don't know. I don't know him. I don't know him. I don't know him. He's a trumpet player. He used to come over here. How long ago? Every one of them died except me. Mm-hm. He had a fellow who used to play a drum with us.

He was operating a cafe and . He had been to anybody . Every one of them died except me. They had a fellow who used to play a drum with us. He was operating a cafe and he ain't been dead by the United States yet. Alexander. He looked better than he did. Yeah. What do you? I was talking to him and he said, you know, one thing you and I got a lot to be thankful for, all the members of our orchestra are dead except you and I. And about a few months after that he died and we had that conversation.
How many nights a week would you work with that band?
About three nights on the average.
Weekends? Middle of the week or what? Most of the weekends. And who did you play for? Mostly for white people. Would you play for societies or parades or anything like that?
Yeah, they were so sorry they haven't been parades. Used to advertise doing trucks, you know. Get on the trucks and advertise for dances.
I've been on a couple of those but you don't see them much anymore. No.
Once upon a time in the Orleans you could see them all around there. You could see three or four of them. Hook wheels. Lock wheels, that's right.
I used to enjoy that. When did the piano come into the bands over here? Well I had a piano player.

Was it I, Miss Nat, who had been here so good, who used to play my band then? Then Grace thought it had been so long I couldn't really say. After you got back from school? Oh yeah, but I played with the Supreme Band. When I organized my own band then I got a piano player, you see.

When did you form your own band, do you remember? Before Depression? After Depression? Before we married. We married in the Depression so it must be. You married forty, forty-one years, is that what you said? Forty-one years ago. Forty-one years ago. Forty-one years ago. So it's been a little while ago. That's a long time to say name, huh? Yeah. Who was that on? We can erase it if you want to, don't worry about it. It's just a joke. That's good publicity. No, but you see, that's the behind it. That's true. That's what I was about to say, though. Don't say that. So you got married about 1921 or something like that? 1921. So you started using pianos before that? Yeah. Before that. Before you were married. Well, did you take them on the trucks with you?
Yeah, we put piano on the truck too. I see.

I've seen sometimes they do that and sometimes they don't. Yeah, we put piano on the truck. They were waiting for them all on the truck, on the corners. Crowds would be waiting for them to pass and they'd have regular street dances and dance to their music. How would you sit on the truck, by the way? We had chairs. But I mean, who'd be in the front of the truck and who'd be in the back?

Well, most of the time the piano and the drummer would be in the back, you see? And the cornet and the trombone would be right at the tail of the truck. In other words, the piano would be in the front, Joe. In the front, yeah.

Right in the back. Back behind you, huh? Yeah. And who would be between the piano and the clarinet and guitar? When did banjos get popular here? Ask Harry, you used to play that. Ask Harry, you used to have banjo play on. You're the first one over here? Or they have them before you? Or, Herbert, what's that boy named Herbert, who? Used to play with the Go Get Them Band. I got him. Yeah, that's when you went to the Go Get Them Band, after him. Yeah. I started after Herbert. You remember that Goldman, the kid in the Goldman? Oh, yeah, yeah. With Paul Maurice? Yeah. I don't know his name, but I don't even know who he's talking. Who did Paul Gorman's sister play with? She played with Celestine. Celestine. Celestine, yeah. Mercedes. Mercedes. I know her. Yes. Mercedes Gorman Fields, her name is, last time I saw her. That's right. I don't know what's happened to her. Oh, she was here this summer. Oh, yeah. That's a lot. I haven't seen her in years. She's from over here? Mm-mm. A brotherly kid. I see. So, you stayed with the Supreme Band for a few years there and formed your own band before you got married, huh? That's right. That's right. I imagine you must have played with the Supreme Band a good eight or nine years.
After you got married, I was thinking, when we got married, it wasn't.
We sure were. You had your own band at the same time?
No. I see.

When you were with the Supreme Band, you didn't play with any other then? No. That's the only band out there. Let's see. Now, we've got to get these years straight in here, because you had so many of them. You got me there. Well, what about the time that the Depression came on? Who were you playing with then? When the Depression hit us? What year was that? 1929. That's right. I guess I was with the Supreme Band then. Still with the Supreme. No, I think you were. So you hadn't formed your own band up then? No. I think I was with the ass on that. Huh? Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. In 29? That's when you went away just about, huh? Sure. Just about. Sure. You were with the Tisdun. When Mr. Cavoey had great the red? Yeah. You were with the first one he had the band. You were with Tisdun.
That's right.
Yeah. Sure, because he had a band with me. We used to come here, remember your daddy? He's so great. Oh, man, you had a band then. I can't remember that.
I'm married in 29, Joe.

It was difficult, because he was all the talk about over here. Oh, man. Something I found. That's all you could hear about. And you know I had made money with you plenty. You played with him for quite a while. Oh, yeah. Yeah. Long years, huh? Long years is right. Bring back members, huh, Harry?
Yes, ma'am, it does. I made money with me, too. That's right.

How many different kinds of clarinets have you owned? Have you owned a C and a B flat and an E flat and all the different kinds, or you always played with one kind? One kind. Which kind is that, a B flat? B flat, E flat. Oh, they're a B flat clarinet like you see today, most of the time. Al but a band? Al but a band. Al but a band. Al but a band. How many keys? Do you remember? I used 13. 13. It's a real old, old one. I used to hold Al without the ring. Yeah. You still have it?

No, I gave it away. I have a brother. I have a brother who teaches at Isaiah University. Oh, yeah? He's been there about, oh, 30 years, almost. He's been a professor here about 30 years. His son was taking up saxophone, you see. And after I gave it up, I brought the clarinet over to him and gave it to him. He said maybe he could make some use of it to see because I wasn't going to play anymore. What was he playing?
What does he teach, I mean? Does he play music? Is that your brother?
No, he teaches manual arts.
Oh, I see. You say your father played anybody else in the family play?
Yeah, my sister played piano but she played classical music. Mm-hmm. I've seen that.

Now what are some of the classical numbers she played, just out of curiosity? That's a little out of my line. Yeah, my daughter could do it. I've seen her class here. I see. Oh, the clarinet. Who made your clarinet? What else? I'll tell you, I forgot. You forgot now, I had Pencil Miller. I believe you had a Selma. I believe you had a Selma. Selma's have just come in style more in late years. Oh, well, it won't be. Thank you. Oh, well, it won't be. Thank you.
I'll put that on here so they'll know. Rio 2, Summoner Labatt, and it's November 11, 1962. We talked about your clarinet there, and while the tape was off, you mentioned that you taught, too.
What did you teach? I taught Taylor and Tri-State College in the Orange. I see. I stayed there for three years. What years were those? Like a few months or three years.
That was 51, 52, and 53. I see. Did you hear any bands in when you were over there, Monta? Or did you just go to work?

Yeah. I go around and listen to bands in this French Quarter. Listen to that cellar stare at them there after I get off from work, you know, sometimes. See, I get off early, I say, I'm going to the French Quarter, listen to that some good jazz music. And what's that white band, the Orphanile, they've been a while in the Orange. Sharky? No, I've been a Sharky too. Dukes of Dixon Land? Dukes of Dixon Land, that was my favorite. They were good during that time. And Famous Doors. Yeah. Yeah, that's where they're playing at the Famous Doors.

We're missing that piano player right now. He's playing with Raymond. Raymond Boyd. He was Raymond Perkins Paul Crawford right now. Yeah. The piano player quit him and came back, you know. He got tired of being away from home. Oh.
Uh huh. Yeah. They had a real Dixieland band though. Couldn't take it from them. I was a young brother. Very good. The old man did the poem they band, I read. He plays the trombone.

Trombone, yeah. And the banjo too, he doubles. Yeah. It's an unusual combination, you very rarely see that. Yeah. What's his name? Jack. Jack Asundalk. Oh yeah, that's right. They said banjo that took him off that night. Yeah, well he goes back, he's coming back on it. He used to play banjo pretty rarely. But back to you, did you play parades over here much? No, you didn't tell me too much about that.
I was on the own carnival.
What kind of carnival do you have over here?
Nice carnival.
What happens?
Well, they have a parade, and right after the parade they have a dance until five o'clock that afternoon, then they resume that night from eight to twelve.
Do they dance in the streets or in the hall? Oh yeah, dance in the streets, in the hall too.
Dance anywhere on the carnival. That's where I can't do it. Yeah, real nice one.

Last carnival we had Indians. I mean they had some beautiful costumes. Yeah, costumes but... Not like the New Orleans Indians, though. Oh, nothing. Oh no. They're wild. They go wild. Yeah, we got tame Indians. They're supposed to get juiced over their ass. I don't have two pistols in their bosom. One, two. That's true. I'm afraid of them. One of my favorite Indian tribes, the chief had one on each side. He made these suits. Of course, every night when you come from work, you wait an hour and a half, two hours on your suit. Every year you have a different suit. They have beautiful suits. Yeah, who was playing with us when... When... I wanted to ask you something and you messed up. Excuse me. It's gone. It's gone. We'll get back to... Yeah, you might think of it while you're talking. While we're talking about it. I've been playing with so many fellas out in New Orleans. Well, who did you hear when you went over there in your younger days when you were just a little bitty boy? Did you go over and hear music then? In New Orleans?

Mm-hmm. Well, I used to listen to, I believe it was the Imperial man with Manuel Réa and Pico. And then... Was Pico playing with us? He was playing the clarinet with Manuel Réa. They used to play at the old fros and I remember most of the time.
Late old NSH Ristar playing. That's right. And you were young then? Yeah.
I used to go up on the Winter Garden. He was Joe Oliver. Joe Oliver played up there. Remember that was Winter Garden.
No, you don't remember. You can't tell that time you remember. And you was a little bit of boy. I was a young man. I was a young man. I wasn't a young man. I remember Shane. A young man.
I'm a young man, Hal.
That's what I did.

I used to go listen to all that bands where I was in the play, you know? My favorite band was Sam Morgan, though. Oh, you like that one of the bands? Oh, yeah. That's the best. That band was my band too. I can say that. I used to stand on the railroad by the station over there. They used to play right for every Monday on the pavilion right up in the station. And I used to stand up there before I'd go to dance. I'd listen to them harmonize, you know? All of Mexicoians? Oh, man, that man had the best dance music you want to hear. That is to my estimation. Did you work with him later? No, but his brother, Isaiah, used to come in and play trumpet with me. His brother used to play trumpet with me. Isaiah Morgan was his man, but I never did play with Sam. What's that Trumont player? Yeah .

After Gallier he got Johnny Dave. I don't know what I mean. He might be a little young. Who? Johnny Dave, I can't remember. What's his age? Johnny Dave was a man when I was a little boy. Oh, he is? He's in the age of that guy. He's still living in the autumn gibbets. You play a band or two. I never met him.
I used to always tell us. In fact, Uncle Buddy, we used to call him Uncle Buddy. He's named Buddy Johnson. And Yank, he used to come out when Buddy couldn't come meet son Yank, I tell you see.
Well, what was the clarinet player's name? Joe Watson. Joe Watson. Joe Watson. Sweet clarinet player, too. What? Yeah, sweet clarinet player.
What?
He gave me one lesson. Go ahead, Joe Watson. Plenty, plenty.

He gave you one lesson. One lesson. Right. You know what? Of course I didn't have this house in the whole house. He was playing, yeah. And I brought him around, yeah, to give him a drink, you know. And he was showing me how the sandlers go, blues go, you know. And he showed me how the fingers and whatnot. Oh, oh. Oh.
That's right. What about, did you know the drummer? The drummer? Yeah. Williams was his name.
Oh. He used to play with Sam. Oh, you're talking about Nolan Williams. Oh, no. He's talking about.

I know he's talking about. Before your time. You know before my time? You don't remember who? Alfred. Alfred. Alfred. That's who it was. Alfred Williams. That's not Nolan. Alfred Williams. Left hand. Nolan. Left hand drummer. That's what it was.

When Ricard died, Ricard Alexis died, his wife died. I went to his way. And Grace Edwards, she used to play piano with me too. And he said, you know who's out there? Alfred Williams. I said Alfred Williams. He said, yeah, don't you know the left hand drummer? He used to play with Sam Morgan. I said, oh yeah. I said, let me see if he knew he knew me. I said, Alfred, come here. He said, you know this man? He said, no. He said, you know see me before, man. He said, no. I don't remember. I said, where you belong from? You ain't been living in Yawnd. He's been out in Texas. That's right. That's correct. And I said, you ever been to Bay of San Jose? He said, hell, I know you know you little but. He was in Texas with Bat Brown. Yeah. That's where I've been the first time in years.
And I saw Stan had another good drummer one time. I mean Sam Morgan. Roy. Oh yeah, Roy. Little Roy Evans. Roy Evans. Do you know him too?
I know his name.

I heard him on the record. Oh boy. I used to practically live with him. You know Sam Morgan, the first one I seen used a clap stick. You know the slap stick? Mm-hmm. When you put that horn down, boy, you got a slap stick. That's right. Slap. Slap stick. He had a band, had kept what you call. Time. Boy's class. I never saw no band keep that good time as Sam Morgan. Well, what about yourself when you developed your style on clarinet? Did you have anybody that inspired you? Nobody but the band. But I mean you didn't try to copy Joe Watson or Teal or anybody, huh? No. Uh-uh. Well who were some of your favorites, or you must have had some favorites among the musicians? Oh, in your hands.

Anywhere. Well we had a clarinet player, yeah he was good himself. And Paul Maurice, he used to play in the Supreme Band. We used to go to the automobile and he'd take everybody out of his attention towards him when he started playing that clarinet. He was good. He'd take parts out of his clarinet.
He was good. Well what about yourself, what kind of style of clarinet would you play? Would you play lead or would you play harmony or what?
No, I would be harmony most of the time. Tell you the truth, I wasn't as good a musician as the musicians would play it with me. But I used to make more money than first class musicians.

Well did you play more notes than the trumpet or less or how'd you work that? Well I played mostly lead with the trumpet you see. In harmony. Yeah. But you wouldn't noodle around a lot or anything? No, very seldom. Oh yeah, you'd play out of range.
Very seldom. Very seldom. Very seldom. Very seldom. Not too much, not like hand in. Oh well no.
Would you compare yourself from the style of Piku or?
Oh no, those men were superior to me 100%. They don't come to a better than them kind men when he was at his prime, you know. I don't know who you take Piku.

You know who Mr. Lopat used to play something like that? He used to play something like Mealy. On that order, Mealy Barnes. But just like Mealy, you know. He had eyesight, he had eyesight. But when I heard him play, that's what all he played. You know Mealy Barnes? Do you know him? I'm probably. He's not brown-skinned. He's not brown-skinned. He's not. I heard that name. Well he used to play with Chris Kelly and all those guys, but he was not steady with those guys. He played with them and all. He played with them and all. He played with Chris Kelly. I remember Chris Kelly used to come in and play all the time, wonderful million years. Oh yeah? Yeah.

Yeah, but Chris when he came there most of the time he was with Ellis. My mother's great. He's come out there most of the time he was with Ellis. My mother's great. Chris Kelly? I didn't know they played together. He's come out there most of the time he was with Ellis.

My mother's great. I didn't know they played together. I didn't know they played together. I don't know, I may be wrong, but I don't think those two ever played together. Chris Kelly? Chris Kelly was selling his name? Well I didn't know him, that's what I said. Oh, Guy Kelly you might be thinking of. Who? Guy Kelly. That's what he was talking about. In fact, I didn't think Chris would play with Sonny Sommers. I didn't think it was two, I don't know, I may be wrong, but I don't think those two ever played together. Chris Kelly? He was a brass band, him and Sonny Sommers. Chris Kelly was a cellist name? Well I didn't know him, that's what I said. Oh, Guy Kelly you might be thinking of. Who? You might be talking about the great Guy. Guy Kelly. That's what you're talking about. Oh, yeah. You're talking about, you're talking about Ace's trumpet man, don't you? I'm wrong. I'm wrong. You're talking about Guy. Yeah, I heard him. You see the reason why I say that, because Chris had a band the Sunset, and he was talking about the Sunset, and he was coming to the Sunset, and he was coming to the Sunset, and he was going to be a guy Kelly Kelly. That's all for Chris and Trump. What kind of trumpet players did you have around here? Would they play the straight lead, a lot of variations?

Oh, they had good trumpet players. They joined because, you know, they'd come to the band here. Oh, yeah. He was first class, good reading and everything. And then I had Kid Ricard, Ricard Alexis. He was tough and easy. And then I had, I had pretty good, what the sugar. Kai ever played with you?
Yeah.
Yeah, we had Kai. And Rene, Kid Rene, and then there's him out there too. But Kai was not from him? No.
No. No. Where's he from, Kai? I wouldn't know. You know why?
And then I had Kid Clay. He was tough too when he was, when he was young. And playing.
Then we all walked that place over there across too. I'll tell you. We went to Mobile once.

I had Clayton, Warren, myself, Bubba, Eddie Thomas, and Sam Williams on Trombone. And we got down on Davis Avenue and everything was the peanut vendor then. And that was our main number. And they said, play the peanut vendor, play the peanut vendor. Excuse me, spread it. Them niggas can't play no peanut vendor. So I said, Jimmy, play Shake It and Break It. Play Shake It and Break It. I said, now I struck the peanut vendor for him. And that was his grip. He really could play it. And Warren could sing it just like Lewis Homer. He could sing it just like Lewis Homer's song. That's what Warren did. And we played the peanut vendor. They took the key out the truck. We was advertising on the truck. They wouldn't let us move. We had to play it again. Well, we moved to the next corner just like a parade. People falling behind the band. And we played at the Eureka Garden that night. Man, they could get this. Lord, that place, it looked like it wasn't standing around. What do you mean that? Well, music was cheap at that time. We got $75 in our expenses. And you want to hire us for the next night. So I said, yeah, we can play. We cost you more money. And I said, it was $100. Give me $50 a party. We'll stay. And give us a place to eat and a place to sleep. So they made me get old Mike and the Nonsense and dance for the next night to see. And the next night it looked like there were more people here at the horse knocking. Who was Bubba? Bubba, he was a banjo player. We had a banjo in our band. Bubba Bush, he lives out in California now. And he was off a banjo player then. How did Clayton play then? Would he play a lot of high notes or low? Yeah, he could hit them high notes. Clayton could blow that on the thing, he could tell you.
Oh, I heard him in late years, you know. Oh yeah. I'm talking about in his early years. He's staying up on that trumpet.

He's going down now. Yeah, he's staying up on that trumpet and blow that trumpet. Would he? He was a good blues player. Yeah. What kind of playing would he feature on the blues? Would he use mutes or? No. He could hit my nose. He could blow that on the other side.
He could blow that on the other side. He could blow that trumpet. Oh yeah. He could blow that on the other side. Did he feature mutes or?
No. Always open. Oh, practically all the time open man.
Did anybody feature mutes over here? Much? Trombone or trumpet?
Oh, geese feature mutes in the trombone. Oh, geese feature mutes in the trombone.
You want to try something on my other back?
No, it's okay.
I got some if you want to try.
Thank you.
What kind of mute would he use or should I ask?
Just shove up in your horn.
Just ordinary mute. No wah-wah. Just ordinary mute. They didn't have much wah-wah mute.
You know one used to use horn mute? Sam Horgan. I never seen a man use mutes like Sam Horgan. He knew what to do with them though. Sam had a good plan.

Yeah, well I know he was good, even with what everybody says. You can tell it on the record but he must have been better, because he made that record in 1927 I think. And I think he'd already had one stroke at least or something. It's hard to tell what he was like. You know? Good. After he had that boy stroke he was dragging. Yeah, he was dragging. That's when he had Skeeter with him. Who's Skeeter? Well, Fusche. That's right. Red boy Alton. Alton. From Mobile, Alabama. I never will forget that. Because he's on Al Fusche. That's right. He's California now, isn't he? Is that right? I think he has a band and he's proud that he's got that Sam Morgan beat. Well. In California, I hear that. Well, I wish I knew what part of California he was like to write. Me too. Santa Barbara. Santa Barbara. Look, do you know he's an address there? No, but I think we could probably. He sacked him up there, wasn't he? Oh, Al Fusche. No, man. That's the man lying there. That's the man lying there. That's the man lying there. That's the man lying there. Every break I know, understand. Really? He learned you every break he knew? I used to go to the Oilers house at 10 o'clock every Sunday morning. And I don't care, sometimes I'd see him in the morning just going in, you see, when I'd be going to the grocery or something and I wouldn't go to his house. Do you know he'd call me up? He said, I don't care what time I come in, he said, I want somebody to play something like me. And I had to go every Sunday morning on Floyd Street. That's right. Third and that man lying there. Third and that man lying there.
Third and that man lying there.
Did he play around here much? With Sam Morgan. He come over with him. I see all of the coast, Buffaloes, Moabill, Sam Morgan and the rural all of that. Oh yeah.
What did you say he used to play over here with Joe Harris? Joe Harris. Joe Harris. He used good sax too, man. He used good sax. He was playing recently but I haven't seen him here.
He used to play with the Amethystogonians, man. He had a stroke.
He had a stroke. Yeah, I was fixing to say that.
He had a stroke. Yeah, I was fixing to say that. He had a stroke. He had a stroke.
Yeah.
I don't know Tex. Tex died in the cradle house, all right.
No, no.
Tex is living. He had a stroke. He told me he died in the cradle house. He didn't die. He was sick.
Other part is all right but he didn't die.

I saw him at the bank with a couple of months or a meeting. Yeah. That Miles there we was trying to figure out what was Tess's name and I couldn't think of him. I knew him. At the same time I was talking about Tiddy Tat, the puzzle of the letter. But I knew I thought about Alexander's name. Yeah, that's his name. He's not Alexander's name. He's not Alexander's name. He's not Alexander's name. He's not Alexander's name. I remember where he is.

One Saturday he came over here to play with my band, with me and we had meatballs and spaghetti for dinner. Tex got drunk and left out there with a spaghetti sandwich. I knew I was trying to go out there. That was one of my biggest spaghetti sandwich in my life. That's a new one on me.
Pagetta sandwich. Oh my goodness.

He went back a time where all that whiskey was, that bootleg liquor was there, you know, and he ripped his pants on the side for you to clean on down there out there. We'll get to come back here with his pants ripped.
He was a good saxophone player too.
He played that good baritone horn.

Dad knows what he's doing with anything he picked up. He said baritone horn, but he was playing that with us in the neighborhood. He could play that baritone horn. He's a good musician. His dad was a good baritone horn player. Yeah. His dad was one of the best. He had to play for one-year-old horn. Yeah. He had to play for one-year-old horn. Yeah. He had to play for one-year-old horn. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. I'm calling him everything. Sumter. Sumter. Sumter. Sumter. Sumter. I thought it was Sumter and La Bada. Sumter. Sumter. Tio used to take me to the hummingbird on Saturday night.
You know Tio, huh? Oh, number one musician Tio was. They were beatin' vocals in there. He was one of the best I ever knew. Yeah, he was a sight reader.
They called you anything besides Sumter? Joe. Joe. I heard him call you Joe.
My name is Joseph Sumter, but most people call me Sumter, you see. My name is Joseph Sumter. And your father was Joseph? Joseph L. Bada. Same here. Same here. Same here.

Well you had an advantage of having a musical father. I'm glad to see you. I just seen how much time I had on. You got some more questions? No, I just saw some of the time I had on tape, so. Yeah, I just thought you had something special. No. Would you say there was much difference in the way the bands here played and the way they played in New Orleans? Yeah, and you just fit right in. There couldn't be too much difference, you know. That's right.

That's right. Did you have it when you were a kid or what? Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. When I was a kid, you didn't have nothing but a brass band. I didn't say that much. I didn't say that much because I didn't play with them fellas out of the audience, you know. Yeah, and you just fit right in.
There couldn't be too much difference, you know.
Yeah, that's right. That's what Dixie played mostly, you know.
Well, when did the ragtime music start up over here? Did you have it when you were a kid or what?
No. When I was a kid, you didn't have nothing but a brass band. Mm-hmm. You didn't have the orchestra. When I come back from school, I found an orchestra, yeah.
And they were playing by head and playing writing stuff and everything?
Well, you see, they played and practiced great music, you know. Oh, yeah. They said, well, when all this jazz came out, they started trying to rag it too.

You know, when the brass band would play for these places where they played for the dance, the brass band would take, like some of them numbers would take the chord of, you know what I mean, the trio, and they played for the dance. Some of them, the trio, some of them brass band, they were so beautiful, you know. They're pretty. Yeah. Well, that's what they do a whole lot of time. But when did the jazz hit over here, the ragtime? Was that around World War I, before or after I won? After. After World War I, it got popped up. Did you make any records, by the way? You know, to be put out? No, I don't believe it. What about you, Harry? No, I never did. You never did. You never did. You never did. You never did. You never did. I can't answer to you. You never did. Just make them for yourself. Yeah, just over my teeth, that's all. I just wish that Clarence Teddude's band had recorded, you know. I wish so myself. We had a band. Oh, at that time. You used to play this new band? Sure. Yeah. Sure. First time we met you, we're not coming over here. You know, we'd go play at the Woodman Hall. Yeah, we'd play at the Woodman Hall. Yeah, we'd play at the Woodman Hall. But our big dance was out there at the Hundred Men for Fee. Hundred Men for Fee. And they still up, Dick. Yes, sir. They still up at the Hundred Men for Fee. And they was kidding me, Joe. They was kidding me. They said, where's all your kinfolk you been telling me about? Oh. And it was kind of getting late, you know. And late on, here come my people. Hundred, yeah. When my people come in there. To fill up the hall. Fill up the hall. When his family come in and take the hall, it got moved. Yeah. I can see it. Yeah. Old days on that, right? Yes, ma'am. What kind of dances did they do when you were young?
Well, the head was good. The head was called the heeling toe.
The heeling toe. The heeling toe. The heeling toe. Oh, yeah. The heeling toe. The heeling toe. The heeling toe. The big apple.
And then the black bottle.
The black bottle.
And then what you call old quadrilla.
Oh, yeah.

The quadrilla. They used to dance the quadrilla. And after the quadrilla. The men would take the quarter downstairs and eat gumbo or ham and salad. Oh, red beans. You see, when you come over here to play, man, they always had a table set for the band.
What's that way you play? You know, at intermission, the band, they always had a table set for the band. You know? What about the shardest, Joe? Yeah.
There's another dancer you'd dance, the shardest. The mazooka? No other. Who's the shardest?
Variety? The shardest, they call it.
Never did a variety over here, huh?

No. Never heard of it either. But the good old standard waltz. Oh, yeah. Oh, that was wonderful. After waltz is here too. I really wouldn't know how to start to play a shardest. What time it would be. That's the truth. I think a shardest, I don't know who was a mustar. Did you say they didn't do mazookas over here? No. The shardest, you know, the music. The music. The music. The music. The music. The music.
The music.

The music. The music. The music. The music. The music. The music. The music. The music. Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher Cher coming down from New York. I don't think the Trist will ever go out. No, it's so easy. It's a good thing that all these people can dance to it, you know. I can do that myself. Like these are the young ones, but old folks, I don't know. That's good exercise. Everybody does it. Yes, indeed. That's good exercise. Everybody does it. What did the brass bands play for besides dancing, the parades? Well, picnics. Picnics? Mm-hmm. Where would you have picnics?
Well, sometimes they'd go to Eskestand or reveal.

Would they have them right on the seashore? Would they be back in the woods or where? Well, they had clubs. Pavilions. They'd have a pavilion? Yes. At that time, it was open pavilions. You see, it wasn't closed at all. It just had the top and the bottom, in other words. I see. And where would they be? Would they be in the woods or on the lakefront? I mean, on the seafront? Most of them would be in the woods. I mean, they went on the picnics. Yeah. There are so many questions I want to ask you. What special days of the year would they have parades over here? You said carnival was big. Yeah, it was big. Big day. Then the societies turned out, you know, different organizations turned out. Some shows. One of the antivacers, you know. St. Mary's Feast Day. What day was that? That was the 15th of August. Every year they'd turn out. The Italian Society would turn out with the brass band.
And then they'd have a big dinner up there. And they'd have dancing out to the dinner. What about 10th of May? Do you have the 10th of May over here?

St. Mary's Feast Day. What day was that? That was the 15th of August. Every year they'd turn out. The Italian Society would turn out with the brass band, and then they'd have a big dinner up there, the Woodinville World Hall, and then they'd have dancing after the dinner. What about 10th of May? Do you have the 10th of May over here, the Oddfellas? No. I have Oddfellas over here. My small branch of them. Masons? Oh, you can count. Yeah, they belong to them. Are most of the people here Catholic? Yeah, most of them are Catholic. What about all you all? I'm Methodist. He's Methodist. That's Harry. And both of the Lamonts. All of them are Catholic. Mm-hmm. My family's Catholic. Mm-hmm. I see. My family's Catholic for what you just left. Mm-hmm. I see. So you have a lot of Catholic people, and they would have parades.
Yeah, the majority of the people live your Catholic.

What about, do you have pleasure clubs? Like in New Orleans, nothing to compare with the Zulus or the Jolly Bunche. All of them. No. Wild men. Yeah. Can I ask a question? Sure. Joe, did you all ever play for any funeral? No. The brass bands? Uh-uh. Never had bands. Well, I see how time is. I often wondered about brass bands. Yeah. Yeah. They had so many different kinds of jobs that were played by brass bands, I know, in the old days. They don't play now. They have that down. Well, it's just about to run a lot of brass bands. Yeah. How dear to dear to dear to dear to dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear We sure do appreciate it. My grandchildren's gathered all around. That's up and grand. That's not me. That is, we have. No, Harry had two minutes. I won't say how many. Harry's got too many. I bet he hasn't got as many as I have. We have. He's young. He's young, yeah.

segments.chapter: Bay St. Louis roots and early music
segments.title: Opening: date, place, names and birth of Sumner Labat
segments.summary: Allen records the date and place, Labat and wife Carmen give names, and Labat gives his birth (1894) and says his father played baritone in the Promo brass band.

segments.chapter: Bay St. Louis roots and early music
segments.title: Instrumentation of his father's Promo brass band
segments.summary: Labat lists the pieces in the Promo society brass band: trumpets, baritone, bass, drums, trombones; no clarinet.

segments.chapter: Bay St. Louis roots and early music
segments.title: The Tio family in Bay St. Louis
segments.summary: Discussion of old man Tio, Lorenzo, Papa Tio and Louis, their local roots and possible Mexican origin.

segments.chapter: Bay St. Louis roots and early music
segments.title: Schooling in Virginia and switching from violin to clarinet
segments.summary: Labat took lessons at school in Rock Castle, Virginia, played violin, later resumed clarinet; he studied tailoring.

segments.title: Forming his own band with New Orleans players
segments.summary: After Supreme Band members died, Labat formed a six-piece band hiring Kid Howard, Kid Rena, Celestin, Willie Humphrey, George McCollum and Johnny Handy, playing mostly jazz.

segments.title: Members of the Supreme Band
segments.summary: Labat names the seven-piece Supreme Band lineup with Paul Maurice on clarinet and himself leading on violin.

segments.title: Joining the Supreme Band after school
segments.summary: Right after World War I Labat auditioned on violin for leader Paul Maurice and joined, staying until the members died.

segments.chapter: Bay St. Louis roots and early music
segments.title: Music at school in Virginia
segments.summary: Labat recalls his years in Virginia, the school orchestra and brass band, and violin lessons from Professor Gadibasio.

segments.title: Members of the Promo Brass Band
segments.summary: Labat names the Promo brass band players, including his father, and dates the band to about 1912.

segments.title: Promo band rehearsals and the Holy Ghost band
segments.summary: The band rehearsed in his father's dining room, played in Mobile, and a related Holy Ghost band played Catholic parades and burials.

segments.title: Tunes Labat played and remembers
segments.summary: Allen asks about music left from his father's time and favorite numbers; Labat names St. Louis Blues and High Society.

segments.title: Where the Supreme Band played and for whom
segments.summary: The Supreme Band played along the coast, Mobile and the Great Southern Hotel, mostly weekends for white audiences and advertised dances from trucks.

segments.title: Piano in the band and seating on the advertising truck
segments.summary: Labat added a piano to his band and describes how the players sat on the dance advertising trucks.

segments.title: Sorting out dates: Supreme Band, own band and the Depression
segments.summary: Allen and the others try to establish when Labat formed his own band relative to his 1921 marriage and the 1929 Depression.

segments.title: His clarinet, family and the instrument's make
segments.summary: Labat describes his B-flat 13-key clarinet, giving it to a nephew, his brother the teacher and his pianist sister.

segments.chapter: Later years and the New Orleans scene
segments.title: Teaching tailoring in the 1950s
segments.summary: Labat taught tailoring at Tri-State College for three years in 1951-53.

segments.chapter: Later years and the New Orleans scene
segments.title: Hearing Dixieland bands in the French Quarter
segments.summary: Working in New Orleans, Labat visited the French Quarter to hear Sharkey's band, the Dukes of Dixieland and the Famous Door.

segments.title: Bay St. Louis carnival parades and dances
segments.summary: Labat describes the local carnival with its parade, street and hall dances, and the milder masking compared with New Orleans Indians.

segments.chapter: Later years and the New Orleans scene
segments.title: Hearing New Orleans bands as a young man
segments.summary: Labat recalls Imperial Band, Manuel Perez and Picou, and Joe Oliver at the Winter Garden.

segments.title: Sam Morgan's band and his drummers
segments.summary: Labat calls Sam Morgan's band his favorite, recalls the Monday pavilion concerts, Isaiah Morgan, Joe Watson's clarinet lesson and drummer Alfred Williams.

segments.title: Labat's own clarinet style and favorites
segments.summary: He played mostly harmony, rarely noodled, praised Paul Maurice and says Picou and others were far superior.

segments.title: Mealy Barnes, Chris Kelly and Guy Kelly
segments.summary: Allen and Labat sort out whether Chris Kelly or Guy Kelly played with local bands.

segments.title: Trumpeters who played with his band
segments.summary: Labat lists trumpeters he hired, including Kid Ricard Alexis, Kid Rena and Kid Clayton.

segments.title: Playing Mobile's Eureka Garden and Clayton's trumpet
segments.summary: A story of a Mobile truck trip where the crowd demanded the Peanut Vendor and the band was rehired at a higher fee; also Clayton's high notes and open playing.

segments.title: Use of mutes among local players
segments.summary: They discuss mute use by trumpet and trombone players and Sam Morgan's skill with mutes.

segments.title: Sam Morgan's later years and his saxophonists
segments.summary: Allen and Labat talk about Sam Morgan's stroke, Skeeter Fusche, Joe Harris and Tex.

segments.title: Tex and the spaghetti sandwich
segments.summary: Labat tells a humorous story of the saxophonist Tex getting drunk at a Saturday dinner.

segments.title: Tio, and Labat's given name
segments.summary: Labat praises Tio as a sight reader and explains he is Joseph Sumner Labat, named for his father.

segments.title: Bands here compared with New Orleans; brass band to orchestra
segments.summary: Labat says local and New Orleans bands were similar, that only brass bands existed when he was a boy and orchestras appeared by his return.

segments.title: Ragtime and jazz arrive; no recordings; dance halls
segments.summary: Allen asks when jazz came, Labat says after World War I; none of them recorded; they recall dance halls.

segments.title: Dances of the period and the band's supper table
segments.summary: Labat names dances such as the quadrille and black bottle, with a meal laid out for the band at intermission.

segments.title: Picnics, feast days and parades
segments.summary: Brass bands played picnics at open pavilions, St. Mary's feast day on August 15 and society parades.

segments.title: Local Catholic majority, no pleasure clubs, and closing
segments.summary: They note the town is mostly Catholic, with no pleasure clubs or funeral bands, and the tape winds up.
